Abstract
Against the backdrop of the replication crisis, quantitative research in human resource management, as in many areas of
the social sciences, relies on instruments and procedures whose legitimacy is often taken for granted. However, closer
examination of how data are produced, interpreted, and justiﬁed reveals a more complex and less unproblematic picture.
Drawing on a systematic review of 398 empirical articles, this paper shows how dominant methodological practices
become standardized and taken for granted, despite their well-documented limitations. Rather than treating these
practices as isolated methodological issues, the article argues that they are embedded in a broader epistemic regime in
which statistical tools contribute to the production of scientiﬁc legitimacy while simultaneously obscuring their own
limitations. In this perspective, practices such as the metric treatment of ordinal scales, the routine use of hypothesis
testing, and the reliance on non-probabilistic samples are not merely technical choices, but mechanisms through which a
performative form of rigor is constructed. The ﬁndings suggest that quantiﬁcation in HRM does not simply describe
phenomena, but actively shapes what can be observed, compared, and asserted. This calls for a more reﬂexive approach
to research methodology, attentive to the epistemic conditions under which knowledge claims are produced.
Introduction
The crises of replicability and reproducibility (Baker, 2016) are not limited to the natural sciences; they also affect the

Abstract
Against the backdrop of the replication crisis, quantitative research in human resource management, as in many areas of
the social sciences, relies on instruments and procedures whose legitimacy is often taken for granted. However, closer
examination of how data are produced, interpreted, and justiﬁed reveals a more complex and less unproblematic picture.
Drawing on a systematic review of 398 empirical articles, this paper shows how dominant methodological practices
become standardized and taken for granted, despite their well-documented limitations. Rather than treating these
practices as isolated methodological issues, the article argues that they are embedded in a broader epistemic regime in
which statistical tools contribute to the production of scientiﬁc legitimacy while simultaneously obscuring their own
limitations. In this perspective, practices such as the metric treatment of ordinal scales, the routine use of hypothesis
testing, and the reliance on non-probabilistic samples are not merely technical choices, but mechanisms through which a
performative form of rigor is constructed. The ﬁndings suggest that quantiﬁcation in HRM does not simply describe
phenomena, but actively shapes what can be observed, compared, and asserted. This calls for a more reﬂexive approach
to research methodology, attentive to the epistemic conditions under which knowledge claims are produced.
